questions.question: Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given. He was sent to a school in Pavia, and there, he was allowed to devote (many of his time) to the subjects which particularly interested him.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.

He was sent to a school in Pavia, and there, he was allowed to devote (many of his time) to the subjects which particularly interested him.
questions.solution: The noun 'time' is uncountable, so the uncountable adjective 'much' should be used to modify it in place of the countable 'many'. Also, the adjective 'most' should be used in place of the adverb 'mostly', as it is being used to modify the noun 'time'. B is the right answer.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. I took the cycle which he buy yesterday.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

I took the cycle which he buy yesterday.

options.text: that which he had buy yesterday
options.html: that which he had buy yesterday

questions.solution:
The plural verb 'buy' cannot be used for the singular subject 'he'. So, the phrase needs replacement.

Option (a) is incorrect as 'yesterday' in the sentence implies past tense, but 'buys' is the present tense verb.

Option (c) is incorrect as 'had' should be followed by the third form of verb, but 'buy' is base verb. 'Bought' would have been appropriate here.

Option (b) makes the sentence grammatically correct.

Hence, option (b) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Jeetu can either open his own institute or join Maheshwari classes.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Jeetu can either open his own institute or join Maheshwari classes.

options.text: either can open his own institute or
options.html: either can open his own institute or

options.text: either can open his own institute nor
options.html: either can open his own institute nor

options.text: can neither open his own institute or
options.html: can neither open his own institute or

questions.solution:
·"Either..or" is a correlative conjunction i.e. both 'either' and 'or' exist together.

·The format of Either..or is:Noun/Pronoun + verb + Either+ the Condition + or + the other Condition.

·For example: You can either take this salary or leave the job.

·As we can see, the format of the question needs no improvement.

·The other options are grammatically incorrect.

·Therefore, the correct answer is:(d) No improvement required.

Additional Information:

·The format of Neither..nor is:Noun/Pronoun + verb + Neither+ the Condition + nor + the other Condition.

·For example: He is neither smart nor hardworking.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. The venomous snake (have delivered) a deadly bite.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

The venomous snake (have delivered) a deadly bite.
questions.solution:
The plural verbs 'have' and 'deliver' cannot be used for the singular verb 'snake'.

Option (b) is incorrect as the helping verb 'has' requires the past participle form (V3) of the verb after it. But 'deliver' is the base verb.

Option (c) is incorrect as 'will' requires base verb after it, and not the -ing form of verb.

"Delivered" is the correct and most suitable choice. It provides the past tense form of the verb, accurately conveying that the venomous snake has delivered a deadly bite. Hence, (a) is the correct answer.

The final sentence: The venomous snake delivered a deadly bite.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement required' as your answer. The world economy needs leadership from the United States of America, as no further nation has more to lose from a collapse of multilateralism.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement required' as your answer.

The world economy needs leadership from the United States of America, as no further nation has more to lose from a collapse of multilateralism.
questions.solution:
The underlined phrase is incorrect because the word 'further' (which, in adjective form, conveys the meaning of being more distant in space than something else of the same kind (or) additional to what already exists) has been used as an adjective to modify the noun 'nation' which renders the phrase meaningless. The correct phrase to be used in the sentence is 'as no other nation has', which makes the sentence grammatically and contextually correct. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

The phrase in option (a) is incorrect because of the use of 'had' (past perfect) while the sentence is of the present perfect form. The phrase in option (b) is incorrect because the word 'while' is used to show contrast but the sentence does not have anything of contrasting nature.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. If you were a chef, you (would have cooked) delicious meals every day.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

If you were a chef, you (would have cooked) delicious meals every day.
questions.solution:
For imaginary sentences, 'were' is used with all the subjects.

Syntax: If + subject + were + object, subject + would + first form verb.

Only option d) has the base form verb 'cook'. The given phrase and option b) have 'have' after 'would' which isn't required, and option a) has 'be' after 'would' which isn't required.

The correct sentence is: If you were a chef, you would cook delicious meals every day.

Hence, option (d) is correct.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Alice and Bob smiled at (one another) across the crowded room, silently sharing a moment of understanding.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the bracketed part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Alice and Bob smiled at (one another) across the crowded room, silently sharing a moment of understanding.
questions.solution:
'Each other' denotes the mutual relationship between people/ things while 'one another' denotes the mutual relationship among more than two people/ things.

Since here only two people are concerned, 'each other' is a suitable option over 'one another' while the other two phrases do not exist.

The correct sentence is - Alice and Bob smiled at each other across the crowded room, silently sharing a moment of understanding.

Hence, option (a) is correct.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Don't forget to use insect repellent to ward away the mosquitoes.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Don't forget to use insect repellent to ward away the mosquitoes.
questions.solution:
The phrase 'ward away' is incorrect. The correct phrasal verb is 'ward off' (prevent someone or something from harming or affecting one). It is grammatically and contextually correct in this sentence. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

Note:

Phrasal verb: A phrase that consists of a verb with a preposition or adverb or both, the meaning of which is different from the meaning of its separate parts. Example: She has always looked down on me. Here, the phrasal verb 'to look down on someone' doesn't mean that you are looking down from a higher place at someone who is below you; it means that you think that you are better than someone.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Despite of the pressure of daily newspaper coverage, the magazine kept itself relevant by doing investigative stories and detailed political analyses.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Despite of the pressure of daily newspaper coverage, the magazine kept itself relevant by doing investigative stories and detailed political analyses.
questions.solution:
'Despite' is not followed by the preposition 'of' as it means without being affected by; in spite of. Usage of the preposition ‘of’ with it is superfluous. But usage of preposition ‘of’ is required after ‘pressure’ to show the possession.

So, only option b) (despite the pressure of) can improve the underlined part of the given sentence.

Hence, option b) is correct.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Peterkin readjusted his hat and was soon listening with as much interest as I was.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Peterkin readjusted his hat and was soon listening with as much interest as I was.
questions.solution: The comparative adjective 'as' should be used in place of 'so'. The uncountable adjective 'much' should be used in place of the countable 'many', as it is being used to modify the uncountable noun 'interest'. D is the right answer.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. You ought to having taken care of your brothers and sisters.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

You ought to having taken care of your brothers and sisters.
questions.solution:
'Ought to' is a modal verb and a modal verb is always followed by a base verb. 'Having' is the present participle (V4) of the base verb 'have'. So, the underlined part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect.

'Had' is the past tense and past participle of the base verb 'have'. So, option (a) is also eliminated. 'Have taken' is the correct choice. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

Note:

Modal verb: A verb used with another verb to express an idea such as possibility that is not expressed by the main verb. The modal verbs in English are "can," "could," "may," "might," "must," "ought," "shall," "should," "will," and "would." They do not change their form (spelling) and they have no infinitive or participle (past/present). Example: I can speak Spanish. Here 'can' expresses the ability of the person to speak (main verb) Spanish. This ability cannot be expressed by the main verb 'speak'.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. All these belong to the family which have flowers in the form of a cross.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

All these belong to the family which have flowers in the form of a cross.
questions.solution:
'Which' is a relative pronoun and the verb after the relative pronoun should be used according to the antecedent. In this case, the antecedent is 'family' which is singular in nature. So, the plural verb 'have' is grammatically incorrect. So, the underlined part and option (b) are incorrect. The expression 'that which' does not bring out a meaningful sentence. 'Has' is a singular verb. So, option (c) is grammatically and contextually correct. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

Note:

Relative pronouns: A relative pronoun is used to connect a clause or phrase to a noun or pronoun. The clause modifies, or describes, the noun. The most common relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that. For example: She is the girl who received the award for bravery from our Home Minister.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. While those symptoms were troubling , they typically resolved within two weeks.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

While those symptoms were troubling, they typically resolved within two weeks.
questions.solution: 'Troubling' refers to something that causes concern, and 'troubled' means disturbed. Since symptoms can only cause concern, and not be concerned themselves, so 'troubling' will be used here. A is incorrect. B is incorrect as the plural verb 'were' should be used here, as we are talking of more than one symptom. C is incorrect as "we're" is short for 'we are', which makes no sense. D is the right answer.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. Unless he is not very cautious with his money, he will run into debt very soon.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

Unless he is not very cautious with his money, he will run into debt very soon.
questions.solution:
'Unless' is used to denote the condition i.e. 'If not'. So, the use of the negative word 'not' with 'unless' is superfluous. So, the phrase 'is not very' needs to be replaced with 'is very' to make the sentence grammatically correct.

Hence, option (c) is correct.
